title: Joseph: One of the Greatest Pictures of Christ
paragraphs:
Joseph: One of the Greatest Pictures of Christ
The Forgotten Son, the Betrayed Savior, and the God Who Still Rewrites Broken Stories
There are moments in Scripture when a story becomes more than a story.
It becomes a mirror.
A warning.
A promise.
A glimpse of Jesus long before Bethlehem.
And few lives in the entire Bible reveal Christ more beautifully than Joseph.
Most people remember Joseph as the dreamer with the coat of many colors.
But Joseph is much more than that.
His story is one of betrayal, rejection, false accusation, suffering, forgiveness, redemption, and ultimate restoration.
It is the story of a beloved son hated by those closest to him.
A righteous man sold for silver.
An innocent sufferer condemned though guiltless.
A rejected savior who eventually becomes the very source of life for those who rejected him.
Sound familiar?
It should.
Because Joseph is one of the clearest Old Testament pictures of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is why his story still grips hearts thousands of years later.
Because deep down, every one of us knows what it feels like to be misunderstood.
Rejected.
Forgotten.
Betrayed.
Wounded by people we loved.
We know the pain of watching life collapse while wondering where God is.
Joseph knew that pain too.
But his story proves something many people desperately need to hear today:
God can take the greatest scandal of your life and transform it into a testimony of His grace.
Because Jesus still rewrites everything.
The story begins in Genesis 37.
Joseph was Jacob's beloved son.
The Hebrew text says Jacob loved Joseph more than all his children.
The favor shown to Joseph ignited jealousy inside his brothers until hatred consumed them.
When Joseph approached them one day, they stripped him of his robe, threw him into a pit, and sold him into slavery for twenty pieces of silver.
The irony is breathtaking.
The one sent by his father was rejected by his brothers.
Centuries later, another beloved Son would be rejected by His own people.
John 1:11 says:
"He came unto his own, and his own received him not."
Joseph's brothers sat down to eat while he cried out from the pit.
The religious leaders did much the same while plotting Christ's death.
The parallels are impossible to ignore.
Yet even this betrayal was not outside God's plan.
What looked like evil was already being woven into redemption.
Many people reading this are living in a pit season right now.
You did not choose it.
You did not deserve it.
You cannot understand it.
And if you're honest, you may even be questioning whether God has forgotten you.
Joseph probably wondered the same thing.
But heaven had not lost track of him.
Not for one second.
Because God often does His deepest work in places that look like abandonment.
The pit led Joseph to Egypt.
Egypt led him to Potiphar's house.
Potiphar's house led him to prison.
Prison led him to Pharaoh.
And Pharaoh led him to the fulfillment of God's purpose.
The places Joseph wanted to escape were actually the roads God was using.
That truth still changes lives today.
Some of the doors you are begging God to open would destroy you if opened too soon.
Some of the delays you resent are protecting blessings you cannot yet see.
Some of the heartbreaks you mourn are preparing a future redemption story that will glorify Christ far more than immediate relief ever could.
The Hebrew word often translated "providence" is connected to the idea of God seeing ahead.
God sees what we cannot.
He sees the famine before it comes.
He sees the prison before the palace.
He sees the cross before the resurrection.
And He sees your future long before you arrive there.
Joseph's suffering intensified when Potiphar's wife falsely accused him.
His integrity cost him everything.
His obedience appeared to make his life worse.
Can you relate?
Have you ever done the right thing only to suffer for it?
Ever obeyed God and still watched your circumstances unravel?
Joseph did.
Jesus did.
The sinless Son of God was falsely accused, mocked, beaten, condemned, and crucified despite perfect innocence.
Isaiah 53:9 declares:
"He had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth."
Joseph suffered unjustly.
Christ suffered perfectly.
Joseph's life points us toward the greater Savior who would come.
Yet perhaps the most powerful moment in Joseph's story happens years later.
The brothers who betrayed him stand before him without recognizing who he is.
The one they rejected has become ruler.
The one they sold now possesses the power to save them.
The one they wounded now holds their future in his hands.
This moment echoes a future reality revealed in Scripture.
The rejected Christ is also the exalted Christ.
The crucified Lamb is now the reigning King.
The One many ignore today will one day be seen by every eye.
Philippians 2:10-11 declares that every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord.
Joseph's brothers expected judgment.
Instead, they received mercy.
They deserved punishment.
Instead, they found grace.
And this is where the Gospel explodes off the pages of Scripture.
Because Joseph says one of the most breathtaking statements in the entire Bible:
"Ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good."
Genesis 50:20
The Hebrew phrase is astonishing.
The brothers "chashav" evil—planned, devised, intended evil.
But God also "chashav" good.
Human evil was real.
Human responsibility remained.
Yet God's sovereign purpose was greater.
The cross reveals the same truth.
The greatest evil ever committed was the murder of the sinless Son of God.
Yet through that very act God accomplished the greatest redemption in history.
Satan saw defeat.
God saw salvation.
The crowd saw execution.
God saw reconciliation.
The disciples saw the end.
God saw the beginning.
This is the heartbeat of "From Scandal to Grace."
Because the Gospel is the ultimate story of God transforming scandal into redemption.
Peter denied Christ.
David committed adultery and murder.
Paul persecuted believers.
The woman at the well carried shame.
The thief on the cross had wasted his life.
Yet Jesus rewrote every one of their stories.
And He still does.
Maybe you are carrying a scandal nobody knows about.
A hidden addiction.
A failed marriage.
A secret sin.
A crushing regret.
A chapter you wish could be erased.
The enemy wants you to believe your story is finished.
Jesus says otherwise.
The same Savior foreshadowed in Joseph stands ready to redeem what seems irredeemable.
The Greek word often translated as repentance is "μετάνοια" (metanoia).
It means a change of mind that results in a transformed life.
The Gospel is not behavior modification.
It is divine transformation.
Jesus does not merely improve broken people.
He makes them new.
That is why Joseph's story still matters.
Because it is ultimately not about Joseph.
It is about Christ.
Joseph points forward.
Jesus fulfills.
Joseph saved Egypt from famine.
Jesus saves sinners from eternal death.
Joseph fed hungry nations.
Jesus declared:
"I am the bread of life."
Joseph forgave those who betrayed him.
Jesus prayed:
"Father, forgive them."
Joseph preserved physical life.
Jesus grants eternal life.
Joseph was a shadow.
Christ is the substance.
Joseph was a picture.
Jesus is the reality.
And perhaps the most beautiful part of all is this:
Joseph did not know how his story would end while he was living it.
Neither do you.
The pit did not look like purpose.
The prison did not look like preparation.
The betrayal did not look like blessing.
But God was writing a story Joseph could not yet read.
Maybe that's where you are right now.
Staring at pages that make no sense.
Wondering why God allowed what He allowed.
Questioning whether redemption is still possible.
Hold on.
The Author is not finished.
The same God who turned a pit into a palace, a prison into a platform, and betrayal into blessing is still working.
The same Christ who conquered the grave is still rewriting lives today.
And maybe that is why you are reading this right now.
Not by accident.
Not by chance.
But because God wants you to know that your story is not defined by what happened to you.
It is defined by what Jesus can do with it.
Be honest.
This may have touched a wound you've been hiding for years.
You never know which soul is one message away from encountering Jesus Christ.
More importantly, your support helps place biblical truth into the hands of people who desperately need hope.
One day you may discover that the chapter you begged God to remove became the chapter He used to reveal Christ most clearly.
